channel.title: Acme: Light News
channel.description: Positive, lighthearted and unusual current news.

item.title: Owls, bees, puffins and hedgehogs are coming to British banknotes
item.description: Britain’s next banknote designs will feature a barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee, Atlantic puffin and European hedgehog. Nearly 500,000 people voted in the Bank of England consultation; the bumblebee topped the poll. The wildlife will gradually replace Churchill, Austen, Turner and Turing.

item.title: Pikachu takes a tour of the International Space Station
item.description: A spacesuit-clad Pikachu plush stars in a European Space Agency video tour of the International Space Station. Astronaut Sophie Adenot uses the yellow visitor to show viewers the station’s sleeping quarters, food storage and water-recycling system.

item.title: A 2,856-pound pumpkin smashes the world record
item.description: British grower Ian Paton’s pumpkin Bagheera weighed 2,856.8 pounds, topping the previous Guinness record by more than 37 pounds. The 65-year-old said the giant fruit drank about 130 gallons of water a day; after its moment in the spotlight, it will become cattle feed.

item.title: Chemists who mastered molecular ‘mirror images’ win Nobel
item.description: Henri Kagan, 95, and Kenso Soai, 76, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discoveries that let reactions favor one of two molecular mirror images. The work solved a century-old puzzle and became crucial to making medicines, where left- and right-handed versions of the same molecule can behave very differently.

item.title: A 50-million-year-old crocodile gets a new identity
item.description: CT scans and more than 300 anatomical comparisons revealed that a crocodile fossil found near Cairo had been misclassified for a century. Scientists named the newly recognized species Herugavialis cairensis, linking Egypt’s deep natural history to the Sphinx and the ancient god Heru.

item.title: Meerkats get pumpkins and cauldrons for Halloween
item.description: Seven meerkats at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo investigated jack-o’-lanterns and witches’ cauldrons prepared by their keepers. The seasonal props are more than decoration: pumpkins and other changing objects encourage the animals to forage, explore and stay engaged with their surroundings.

item.title: Antarctic ‘ghost particle’ hunter wins the physics Nobel
item.description: Francis Halzen, 82, won the Nobel Prize in Physics for turning a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice into the IceCube observatory. Its buried sensors catch faint traces of high-energy neutrinos—elusive cosmic messengers that pass through Earth and can point scientists toward exploding stars and black holes.

item.title: The Hollywood sign has a secret wild side
item.description: The closed hillside around Los Angeles’ Hollywood sign doubles as an urban wildlife refuge. Hawks sail above the letters, snakes curl at their base, bobcats roam nearby and coyotes leave tracks along the trails. Griffith Park supports about 200 bird species, 50 kinds of butterflies and 40 mammal species.

item.title: Snow leopard cub Sarka makes her Bronx Zoo debut
item.description: Four-month-old Sarka has passed her physical exams and vaccinations, clearing the snow leopard cub to explore the Bronx Zoo’s Himalayan Highlands with her mother, Dariga. The zoo has bred more than 80 snow leopards since 1903 and participates in a program that helps preserve the vulnerable species’ genetic diversity.

item.title: Three scientists win medicine Nobel for controlling cells with light
item.description: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the Nobel Prize in medicine for optogenetics, a method that uses light-sensitive proteins as switches inside cells. The technique lets researchers turn specific neurons on and off with light, opening new ways to study the brain.

item.title: Houston Zoo welcomes a tiny parade of rare reptiles
item.description: Houston Zoo is celebrating several pint-sized conservation milestones, including its first-ever Hosmer’s spiny-tailed skink birth. New arrivals also include star tortoises, eyelash vipers and leaf-tailed geckos—an appropriately scaly cast for October.

item.title: Mars, a crescent moon and a star cluster share the morning sky
item.description: Early risers can see Mars close to a slim crescent moon before dawn on Oct. 5. The red planet is also heading toward the Beehive Cluster, a sparkling group of stars also known as M44, making binoculars especially rewarding over the next several mornings.

item.title: Manila church fills with wagging tails for annual pet blessing
item.description: Dogs, cats and other companions crowded Manila’s Malate Church for a cheerful annual blessing tied to the feast of St. Francis of Assisi. Priests sprinkled holy water over pets and their people as parishes marked the patron saint of animals with one of the calendar’s most photogenic traditions.

item.title: Steve Reich reflects on making music at 90
item.description: Composer Steve Reich, now 90, talks about his latest work and a creative life that helped redefine modern music. The interview finds him still composing, still revising his methods and still thinking carefully about what technology can—and cannot—contribute to human expression.

item.title: Zoo’s first porcupette gets the name Bramble
item.description: Visitors voted to name Point Defiance Zoo’s first porcupette “Bramble,” a nod to her prickly quills and curious nature. Born Aug. 17 to first-time parents Quillow and Nigel, the tree-climbing youngster is thriving and marks the first porcupine birth in the Tacoma zoo’s 121-year history.
